edit.before: No em or en dashes anywhere in a request.
edit.after: Do not use hyphens or dashes in a request.
edit.reason: Simplifies the instruction by replacing technical terms with plain language.

issues: {"type":"clarity","description":"The edit changes 'em or en dashes' to 'hyphens or dashes', which may confuse readers since em dashes ( - ) and en dashes (–) are distinct from hyphens (-). The original phrasing is more precise as it distinguishes between the two types of dashes explicitly.","suggestion":"Consider reverting to the original phrasing or clarifying the distinction between hyphens (-) and dashes (em/endashes) if the intent is to prohibit all three."}

suggestions.what: Add a clear, prominent **‘Request Structure’** heading before the ‘The fields’ section, followed by a concise summary of the key components (label, title, description, kind, group, access) in a bulleted list for quick visual scanning.
suggestions.why: First-time visitors may struggle to locate or understand the core request fields amidst the dense text. A dedicated heading and list improves readability and guides users to the most critical information upfront.

suggestions.what: Reorganise the **‘Groups’** section to use a table format (columns for *Group*, *Purpose*, and *Example URL*) instead of a list, with a brief introductory line (e.g., *“Select your group from the list below”*) to clarify its purpose.
suggestions.why: Tables are more scannable for categorical data like this, reducing cognitive load. The current list format risks overwhelming users with unstructured text, especially for those unfamiliar with the system.

suggestions.what: Separate the **‘People and privacy’** section from the procedural ‘How a request is made’ text with a visual divider (e.g., a horizontal rule or a subheading like *“Privacy & Consent”**) and shorten the introductory sentence to *“Requests avoid naming private individuals.”**
suggestions.why: The two topics (privacy principles vs. workflow) are distinct but currently blended, potentially confusing visitors. A clearer separation and tighter phrasing improve focus and flow.
